confusing.why: The hero says an agent has three parts (model, tools, memory). Step 1 then says her agent has six parts. A newcomer will ask which count is right.
Tokens are used in the log before the callout explains what a token is.
The steps never say where Logs is in n8n, or how to paste each key into its credential. A newcomer gets stuck at step 2.
The zoom idea is never shown, so the three quotes read like rival definitions rather than one idea.
Agentic system, workflow and agent appear within one paragraph, and the difference is not clear until the table.
The Learn text says the key is loaded, but this line passes no key. The reader only learns that the client reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the quiz feedback.
The promise is not kept: kernel is first named in this sentence and only explained far down, under If something breaks.
The lesson says to install packages in a virtual environment but never shows how to create or activate one.
Competitors are never named. Step 5 introduces model-A, model-B and model-C as placeholders only in its code.
The doubled braces are needed inside an f-string, but the lesson never says so, so the reader thinks they are a typo.
Why api_key="ollama" is needed (the client insists on a value, and the local server ignores it) is explained only in the quiz feedback.
client is used here, but this lesson never creates it. The reader has to guess that it comes from Lesson 3.
The code below is a Python dictionary, not JSON. Lesson 6 later says the difference matters, but this lesson does not.
**arguments is used before anyone explains it. Only Lesson 6 gives the explanation.
The grid lists push.py as a file, but the project package has no push.py (only app.py, context.py and tools.py), so the reader cannot find it.
No code shown in the lesson prints this line, and the push function prints nothing. The optional-Pushover note also has no code to match.
The quiz rewards the globals() lookup, but the callout says not to use it on a public app. Step 5 then deploys a public app.
The trap is named, but 'accuracy' and why the last 10 percent is costly are never explained before this list.
'Pilot' and 'vendor' are used in the trap list without a definition, so a newcomer has to guess what they mean.
The lesson says to judge by one number but never shows what such a number looks like.
Mr Tan is never introduced. The story only names Mdm Rohani, Devi and the kopi, so a newcomer does not know who he is or why he has a favourite.
Jason appears for the first time in the closing callout, with no introduction. Newcomers cannot tell whether he is a person or a system.
Step 1 says three things, but Step 2 and the diagram list five decisions. A reader cannot tell how three becomes five.
The lesson opens on terms it never explains (large language model, retrieval, latency). Ironically, that is the exact problem the lesson is about.
AI agent appears for the first time here, with no explanation. Failure modes is also new.
The table is English only, so a 中文 reader gets the rows with no explanation. The phrase data leaves us is also unclear.

confusing.where: Step 2, intro line above the sorting game
confusing.why: The sorting game shows four tasks, so a careful reader stops to ask where the fifth one went.
The title says AI and agents, but the lesson never says what an agent is, so the link between the helper and the word agent is missing.
The answer option says 'Read it through', but the explanation said 'a quick read', so I could not tell whether a summary needs a glance or a full read.
A newcomer does not know why a supplier would change the model, so the 'plan B' in Step 4 has no reason behind it.
It is surprising, and no reason is given.
The $2,400 appears from nowhere. I cannot see how it was counted, and the $3,000 overtime figure needs the $30 an hour from the game in Step 2.
The sort game uses the words hard saving and soft benefit, but the Learn text never names the two groups as a pair, so soft is only implied.
ROI is in the title but never spelled out in English. The 中文 says 投资回报率, so the English reader is left guessing.
The analogy is good, but the reader is never told which hawker role matches which layer, so they have to guess the mapping.
GPU is never explained, and a bank offering a cloud reads like a finance product, which confuses the vendor story.
API is used without a definition, so a newcomer cannot tell what closed means in practice.

The sorting game in Step 1 puts auto-filling supplier invoices under Now, as a known tool with clear hours saved. Here the same work is an uncertain experiment, so a newcomer cannot tell which is righ
Jason is not introduced anywhere in this lesson or in its story, so the analogy names a stranger.
The shelf-label project is never named. The reader cannot tell what it is or whether it is the Step 1 price-label pilot.
Model size and cost are used as if they were the same idea, but the lesson never said what makes a model big or why it costs more per call.
A specific '10 times' reads like a law of nature, but the lesson gives no source for it.
'Price per unit of ability' is vague and 'frontier models' is never explained.
'Underneath' is used here for the first time. Nothing before it says a tool you buy can run on a model bought from a different company, so the risk behind the question is not clear.

confusing.where: Side case and 'What I got wrong'
confusing.why: The callout says Mr Tan caught three slips, but the story never shows her wanting a one-year deal. A newcomer cannot tell what the mistake was.
'Plumbing' is a metaphor used without explanation, and 'searchable knowledge' is unclear to someone new to AI.
The word 'prompt' is used as if I already know it. The sorting game then uses 'Better prompt' as one of its three answers, so I could not sort anything without knowing what it means.

confusing.where: Step 4 · Combine them, and ask for proof
confusing.why: Mr Tan appears here for the first time, with no role. I only learn later, in the warning box, that he made a mistake in his first week.
The hero says 'Devi's team', but the story never says who Devi is. I do not know if Devi is a builder, a boss, or someone else.
A newcomer does not yet know what the model is or what a paid call to it means, so the cost list starts with a word they cannot place.
Read literally it sounds like a table row, and the 中文 reads like a word-for-word translation of that phrase.
Step 2 said S$0.30 is the whole task cost, and checking time was never priced. The quiz then counts checking inside the same S$0.30, so the numbers do not match.
The boxes were drawn as a straight chain Goal, Pick a tool, Look at result, Decide next, with no arrow back. The caption says it is a loop, so the picture and the words disagreed.
Devi, Mr Tan, Jason and Auntie Lim are named before the reader knows who they are. Only Mdm Rohani is introduced.
HDB and the Singapore setting are not explained. A reader outside Singapore may not know what HDB estates are.
The value is said to be dollars or hours, but the table shows plain numbers like 4 and 5. The scale (1 to 5) and the direction (is a high effort mark good or bad?) are never stated.
The lorry is meant to show partnering, but hiring a lorry is buying a service, which is the same as buy. The analogy does not separate partner from buy.
Payback date is used as a known term and never explained. A newcomer does not know it means when the money comes back.
A new shop name appears out of nowhere. The story calls it 'the mart' run by Mdm Rohani, so a newcomer wonders if this is a different company.
Five roles are listed, but the product owner is never named. The reader has to guess that Auntie Lim is the product owner.
The lesson defines this role as guarding data and risk. Money is a different thing, so the two lines do not match.
